title.narrative: Building with Nature Indonesia: Securing eroding delta coastlines

description.narrative: 1. Summary: “Cumulatively, about nine kilometres of permeable structures were deployed along the Demak coast in collaboration with the Indonesian government. Constructed from indigenous brushwood and bamboo affixed to poles, these structures aimed to eventually be supplanted by a restored mangrove belt, which would naturally provide defense against erosion. However, the journey was not without setbacks. A number of structures suffered damage from shipworms or storms, some proved unsustainable in certain conditions, and ongoing maintenance was required. To enhance their durability, modifications in design and materials were introduced. Despite challenges, these structures fulfilled their role by arresting erosion, slowing marine encroachment, and preventing land loss.The initial goal was for new mangroves to take root and flourish in the sediment trapped behind these permeable structures. While this was achieved in certain areas with mangroves reaching up to a meter in height, a new issue emerged in 2017. Newly established mangroves began disappearing, and monitoring poles became submerged. The underlying problem was identified as land and foreshore subsidence, particularly concentrated in the western part of the project area towards Semarang city but spreading across the Demak coast in eastward direction. Groundwater extraction, predominantly by industries and along highways, compacted the underlying soil layers, causing land surface lowering. This development posed a considerable setback to the coastal restoration efforts. Despite this, the permeable structures successfully captured sediment, mitigating and slowing down erosion and land loss. However, substantial reduction in subsidence is essential for mangroves to make a full-scale return. Consequently, the maintenance of these structures might need to extend beyond initial estimates. Nonetheless, the achievements are tangible, resulting from the collective actions of the local participants. Beyond physical labour, these communities engaged in planning activities, proposed structural enhancements, and advocated for protective regulations for the newly reclaimed land.” (Source: Building with Nature, Final Report, Ecoshape et al. 2024)2. Results achievedCommunity engagement, training, awareness and active participationIn total, ten community groups actively participated, relinquishing unproductive ponds and safeguarding newly established mangrove basins from reversion to aquaculture. Financial incentives were sometimes provided for transitioning to alternative livelihoods or renting ponds outside the greenbelt zone. This led to the successful recovery of significant pond areas for mangrove greenbelts, surpassing program targets. However, challenges persist in establishing a continuous coastal greenbelt due to the scattered nature of restoration and the need for broader community involvement.The notion of "Bio-rights" played a pivotal role, where communities received financial and technical support for adopting sustainable aquaculture practices in exchange for engaging in conservation and restoration efforts. The success of this initiative was reflected in a threefold increase in aquaculture-derived income for farmers, who adopted better practices over 464 hectares of ponds.Moreover, the restored mangroves offered manifold benefits beyond conservation, including coastal protection, firewood, fertilizers, nursery and feeding grounds for wild fish, and potential economic opportunities in non-timber forest products. The shift in perspective led communities to actively manage their ponds in ways that contributed to mangrove restoration, coastal protection, and enhanced biodiversity.Ten Community groupsThis transformation manifested in the formation of the Bina Noto Segoro (Bintoro) Community Group Forum, uniting ten community groups under a common goal of "managing the sea." Bintoro spearheaded restoration and livelihood initiatives, advocated for community interests to local governments, and published independent coastal assessments. By project's end, personal stories from aquaculture farmers underscored the substantial impact of the Bio-rights mechanism on their lives and communities.To ensure the project's sustainability, extensive efforts focused on raising awareness about the "Building with Nature" principles and fostering a supportive policy environment. Community engagement played a pivotal role in this endeavour. Coastal field schools and Bio-rights incentives empowered community members to engage in policy dialogues at various levels, resulting in increased appreciation for mangroves' value and services. This was reflected in local restoration efforts, new protective regulations, and commitments to sacrifice aquaculture ponds for mangrove rehabilitation. Building with Nature principles were formally integrated into village development plans and local regulations, attracting government support and increased funding.The project also successfully initiated dialogues on subsidence issues from local to national levels, resulting in development roadmaps with the potential to prevent flooding and erosion on a larger scale. Despite challenges posed by the pandemic, these dialogues continued in 2021, culminating in the Assessment and Roadmap towards Adapting and Mitigating Land Subsidence in Semarang and Demak launched in May 2021.Success factors: replication and scalingThe success of Demak served as an inspiration for innovation, showcasing the potential of nature-based solutions. This approach, exemplified in Building with Nature, found application not only in Indonesia but also gained international recognition. The principles demonstrated in Demak were deemed universal and applicable to various environments, emphasizing the synergy between engineered and natural solutions for climate resilience. The replication of the initiative in other Indonesian regions, endorsement by governmental bodies, and engagement in international events attested to the initiative's significance in addressing climate-related challenges.The initiative's impact extended to capacity building through training programs and curriculum integration at universities, reaching over 2,500 students. The success of the Training of Trainers model laid the foundation for broader implementation in Indonesia and beyond, fostering interest from countries like Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, and Singapore.The project FDW14 RI14 Building with Nature Indonesia: securing eroding delta coastlines is a fundamental part of a broader umbrella programme in Indonesia, targeted at implementing Building with Nature in Demak and replicating and mainstreaming of the approach in different coastal environments. This multi-pronged and staged approach, with complementary projects (with individual sets of activities and target values) that contributed to one overall programme of work helped us to reach an ambition level that would not be attainable through a project-by-project approach.

This project aims to enhance the resilience of 70,000 vulnerable people by implementing a building with nature pilot project, which provides coastal security and supports revitalization of at least 6,000 ha of aquaculture ponds along a 20 km shoreline.

comment.narrative:
Safety depends on establishment of a coastal mangrove greenbelt along the entire coastline in the project area of Demak. To restore mangroves we are 1) restoring the sediment balance by placing permeable dams (target 90 ha of mangroves); 2) converting ponds back to mangroves (target 50 ha of mangroves) and 3) inspire others to follow suit. Re 1) Sedimentation rates behind the permeable structures are good and mangroves begin to recover. However, subsidence is counteracting progress and we now notice that it is much more severe than anticipated. Impact is being studied. Re 2) Communities have agreed to give up 50 ha of ponds, which is a great success. Restoration starts this year. Re 3) KKP and PUSAIR are also placing permeable structures in Demak in eroded areas. We are stepping up our communications in Demak. Success with 1 and 2 will help others to follow our example. This takes time.
424 hectare of ponds as supported by the biorights incentive mechanism
6000 ha safe: We may have reached a threshold where coastal restoration and aquaculture revitalisation in Demak may no longer be feasible at the landscape scale due to the severity of subsidence. Our assumption was that we could reduce coastal erosion and flooding by restoring mangroves to attenuate waves and currents, ultimately reducing flood extent once a wider greenbelt would have been established at the land-scape scale. However, strong subsidence in the Demak project area, especially in the Western part towards Semarang, is progressively rendering large swaths of land and villages below sea level. Although permeable structures and/or mangroves may still buffer against waves and may reduce erosion locally, they will not block water from flowing into the ever lower lying hinterland with high tides.

comment.narrative: The target includes both direct and indirect beneficiaries of the project interventions. The immediate outcome of the project covers an area of 20 km2 that is protected by coastal erosion and inundation. However, due to soil subsidence, the impact of the project measures on the total number of people benefitting is restricted. At least 13500 people will benefit from the project results in 10 communities. Indirect positive effects are still in the range of 70000 people.
